full_judgment: 18. In this case the plaintiffs have come to the court with the assertion that the disputed land was settled with them by the owners of the land on the basis of the Kabuliyat Ext.3 (a) and produced the Dakhilas Ext. 4 series in proof of the fact that the Kabuliyat was acted upon on subsequent payment of rent in pursuance of the said settlement. According to section 101 of the Act, as referred to above, it is for the plaintiffs to prove that as a matter of fact, settlement was granted by the owners of the land and the rent receipts Ext. 4 series were really genuine and represented the correct state of things, as the plaintiffs desire the Court to believe on the said assertion. The burden of proof as to the genuineness of the Dakhila Ext. 4 series is undoubtedly upon them in the absence of any legislative provision to the contrary. There having been no legislative enactment requiring the Dakhilas, Ext. 4 series, which had been formally proved at the trial of the suit, to be accepted as genuine documents, merely on proof thereof there is no question of shifting the onus upon the defendants. The learned Judges of the High Court appear to have been under a misapprehension as to the real effect of formal proof of a document in a Court of law. A private document cannot be taken notice of and marked as an Exhibit without any formal proof, unless the requirement of such proof is waived by the opposing party. The marking of the said document as an exhibit may however, give rise to a belief that it bears the writing or signature of a per-son, as has been deposed to by the witness who proves the said document. The question as to whether the document is a genuine one or it represents the true state of affairs is a question of fact which is to be decided by the Court concerned in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case. There is no legal presumption which the Court is bound to make in respect of such a document. There may be cases where the law requires that the content’s of particular document shall be presumed to be correct unless they are rebutted by adducing evidence by a party who disputes their correctness, as has been provided in Section 103B of the Beagal tenancy Act and Section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. There is no such law as requires a Court to presume that a rent receipt purported to be granted by a land-lord in favour of a certain person is genuine and what has been written in such a rent receipt are true. The learned Judges of the High Court have apparently made a mistake in taking the view that as soon as the rent receipts have been proved the primary onus of the plaintiffs has been discharged and the defendants having failed to produce any rebutting evidence the said rent receipts should have been accepted as genuine and relied upon. The onus of the plaintiffs cannot be discharged until the court is persuaded to accept the position that there had been payment of rent by the tenant and acceptance thereof by the landlord, as a matter of fact, on the basis of the disputed rent receipts. In this case, both of the courts of fact have decided the question of genuineness of the disputed rent receipts in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and have also examined their various features with reference to the surrounding facts and came to the definite finding as to their spurious character. Such a finding is binding upon the High Court in a Second Appeal unless it could be shown that the said finding had been vitiated by an error of law or procedure which had affected the merits of the case. The learned Judges of the High Court do not appear to pay much attention to the views of the Court below as to the several suspicious features which had been specifically referred to in the judgment of the said Courts but appear to have been influenced in their decision by a wrong view of the law as to the burden of proof. The learned Judges were not correct in the view that the lower appellant court discarded the said rent receipts only on the ground of non-production of counterfoils of the said rent receipts. The question whether a particular rent receipt, proved by a party may, be accepted without the production of the counterfoil of the said rent receipt is a question of fact and depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. Under the circumstances, the learned Judges of the High Court exceeded their jurisdiction wider section 100 of the Act in refusing to accept the concurrent finding of fact of the courts below as to the spurious character of the Dkahilas Ext. 4 series.
